pages.body:
Place a book on a table and push it gently. It slides, then stops. Now place a coin on a smooth card over a glass and flick the card away quickly. The coin drops into the glass.

- What made the book start to move, and what made it stop?
- Why do you think the coin did not fly away with the card?

Everything that starts to move, speeds up, slows down or changes direction has been acted upon by a force. In this lesson we define force, compare balanced and unbalanced forces and study the property of objects called inertia.

We begin by describing what a force is and what it can do.

pages.title: What a force is
pages.body:
A force is a push or a pull. Forces are measured in newtons, written N. A force can make a stationary object start to move, make a moving object speed up, slow down or stop, change the direction of a moving object, or change the shape of an object, as when you squeeze a sponge. Common forces include the push of your hand, the pull of gravity, friction between surfaces, the pull of a magnet and air resistance.

Next we study what happens when more than one force acts on an object.

pages.title: Balanced and unbalanced forces
pages.body: Forces usually act in pairs or groups. When two forces on an object are equal in size and opposite in direction, they are balanced forces. Balanced forces cancel each other, so the object does not change its motion. A book resting on a table is acted on by its weight downwards and the push of the table upwards. These are equal, so the book stays still. In a tug of war between two equally strong teams, the rope does not move.

When the forces on an object are not equal, they are unbalanced forces. The object is acted on by a resultant force in one direction, and its motion changes. If you push a stationary football, the push is larger than friction and the ball moves. If a footballer kicks a rolling ball in the opposite direction, it slows down or reverses.

questions.q: Define force and state the unit in which it is measured.

parts.a: A force is a push or a pull, measured in newtons (N).

ideas.t: A force is a push or a pull
It is measured in newtons (N)

questions.q: Define a force.

parts.a: A force is a push or a pull.

ideas.t: A push or a pull

questions.q: State one difference between balanced forces and unbalanced forces.

parts.a: Balanced forces cancel so motion does not change; unbalanced forces change the motion of an object.

ideas.t: Balanced forces are equal in size and opposite in direction, so they cancel and motion does not change
Unbalanced forces are not equal, so there is a resultant force and motion changes

pages.body:
[[pic: Two diagrams of a rope in a tug of war. In the first, two teams pull with equal arrows in opposite directions and the rope stays still. In the second, the left team has a longer arrow and the rope moves left. Label balanced forces and unbalanced forces.]]

| **Balanced forces** | **Unbalanced forces** |
|---|---|
| Equal in size and opposite in direction | Different in size, or not opposite |
| Resultant force is zero | There is a resultant force |
| No change in motion, so the object stays at rest or keeps moving at steady speed | The object starts, stops, speeds up, slows down or changes direction |
| A parked car, a book on a table | A car accelerating, a ball being kicked |
Here is a simple activity to show how unbalanced forces cause motion.

questions.q: State the difference between balanced forces and unbalanced forces.

parts.a: Balanced forces are equal in size and opposite in direction so the resultant is zero and motion does not change. Unbalanced forces are unequal so there is a resultant force and the motion changes.

ideas.t: Balanced forces are equal in size and opposite in direction, so they cancel and motion does not change
Unbalanced forces are not equal, so there is a resultant force and motion changes

questions.q: Two forces that are equal in size and opposite in direction are
questions.e: When two forces on an object are equal in size and opposite in direction, they are balanced forces.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Demonstrating that unbalanced forces cause motion

pages.title: Demonstrating that unbalanced forces cause motion
pages.body:
1. Place a toy car on a smooth table and mark its starting position.
2. Push the car gently with one finger. Notice that the car moves only while the push is greater than friction.
3. Push harder and compare how quickly it moves. A larger unbalanced force produces a greater change in motion.
4. Place a small obstacle in its path and observe what happens when the obstacle exerts an opposing force.

Finally we explain why the coin stayed behind in the opening activity.

pages.title: Inertia
pages.body:
Inertia is the tendency of an object to resist any change in its state of rest or of motion. A body at rest tends to stay at rest. A moving body tends to keep moving at the same speed in the same direction. This is why the coin stayed in place when the card was flicked away, and why you lean forward when a vehicle suddenly brakes.

The mass of an object is a measure of its inertia. A heavily loaded wheelbarrow is much harder to start moving and much harder to stop than an empty one, because it has more mass and so more inertia.
[[pic: Demonstration of inertia. A coin on a card on top of a glass. A hand flicks the card sideways and the coin falls straight into the glass. Label the card, the coin and the glass.]]

questions.q: Explain why a loaded wheelbarrow is harder to start than an empty one.

parts.a: A loaded wheelbarrow has more mass and so more inertia, so it is harder to start moving and harder to stop than an empty one.

ideas.t: It has more mass
So it has more inertia, resisting any change in motion

questions.q: Describe one activity that shows that unbalanced forces cause motion.

parts.a: Push a toy car on a smooth table: it moves when the push is greater than friction, and a harder push makes it change its motion more quickly.

ideas.t: Push a toy car or object
It moves when the push is bigger than friction (unbalanced force); a larger force gives greater change

questions.q: The tendency of an object to resist a change in its motion is called
questions.e: Inertia Inertia is the tendency of an object to resist any change in its state of rest or of motion.

questions.q: What is inertia?

parts.a: Inertia is the tendency of an object to resist any change in its state of rest or of motion.

ideas.t: The tendency of an object to resist change
In its state of rest or motion

pages.body:
Roll a ball on the classroom floor and watch how far it goes. Then roll the same ball on a rough mat, and then on a smooth tiled surface. Compare the distances.

- On which surface did the ball roll the farthest, and why?
- What do you think would happen if there were no friction at all?

In the last lesson we saw that unbalanced forces change motion and that objects resist such changes. These ideas were gathered into a law by the scientist Sir Isaac Newton. In this lesson we state Newton's First Law and explain what it means.

We begin by stating the law carefully.

pages.title: Statement of the law
pages.body:
Newton's First Law of motion states that an object at rest remains at rest, and an object in motion continues to move in a straight line at constant speed, unless it is acted on by an unbalanced force. The law is also known as the law of inertia. Newton published it in 1687 in his book Principia Mathematica, building on earlier work by Galileo.

Now we look at the two parts of the law separately.

questions.q: State Newton's First Law of motion.

parts.a: An object at rest remains at rest, and an object in motion continues to move in a straight line at constant speed, unless it is acted on by an unbalanced force.

ideas.t: An object at rest stays at rest
An object in motion continues in a straight line at constant speed
Unless acted on by an unbalanced force

questions.q: Why is Newton's First Law also called the law of inertia?

parts.a: Inertia is the tendency of an object to resist any change in its state of rest or motion, which is exactly what the first law describes.

ideas.t: Inertia is the tendency of an object to resist change in rest or motion
The first law describes this behaviour

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Explaining the two parts of the law

pages.title: Explaining the two parts of the law
pages.body:
- An object at rest stays at rest. A book on a desk does not slide off by itself. It will move only if something pushes or pulls it.
- An object in motion stays in motion in a straight line at the same speed. A ball moving in space with nothing to slow it would continue forever. On Earth, objects slow down only because of forces such as friction and air resistance.

Some learners think that a moving object needs a force to keep it moving. We now clear up that idea.

pages.title: Why things on Earth seem to stop
pages.body:
When you roll a ball along the ground it slows down and stops. This is not because moving things naturally stop. Friction between the ball and the ground is an unbalanced force that acts against the motion. On a very smooth surface, there is less friction, so the ball rolls farther. If there were no friction at all, the ball would never stop. This is the key idea behind the law.

| **Surface** | **Friction** | **Distance the ball rolls** |
|---|---|---|
| Rough mat | Large | Short |
| Concrete floor | Medium | Medium |
| Smooth polished tile | Small | Long |
| An imagined surface with no friction | None | Would never stop |
[[pic: Three drawings of a ball rolling along a rough mat, a concrete floor and a smooth tile with arrows showing friction getting smaller and the distance rolled getting longer.]]

questions.q: Explain why a ball rolling on the ground eventually stops.

parts.a: Friction between the ball and the ground is an unbalanced force that acts against the motion, so it slows and stops.

ideas.t: Friction between the ball and the ground is an unbalanced force acting against the motion
So the ball slows down and stops

questions.q: Describe what would happen to a moving ball if there were no friction.

parts.a: It would never stop; it would keep moving in a straight line at constant speed.

ideas.t: It would never stop
It would move in a straight line at constant speed

questions.q: A learner pushes a trolley and says it needs a continuous push to keep moving. Use Newton's First Law to correct the learner.

parts.a: By the first law a moving object keeps moving at constant speed unless an unbalanced force acts. The trolley slows because friction acts against it, so the push is only needed to overcome friction.

ideas.t: A moving object keeps moving at constant speed unless an unbalanced force acts
The trolley slows because of friction
The push is needed only to overcome friction

pages.body:
To finish the lesson we use research to build understanding of the law.

## Research task

1. Use your library or the internet to find the words of Newton's First Law in at least two sources.
2. Compare the wordings. Which words are the same in all of them?
3. Write the law in your own words and give one example from your community.
4. Share your findings with the class and decide which wording is clearest.

> **Did you know?** Spacecraft such as probes sent to far away planets travel for years with their engines off. Because there is almost no friction in space, they keep moving at nearly constant speed in a straight line, just as the first law predicts.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: A metal ball on a smooth surface

pages.body:
You are standing in a moving tro tro or bus. The driver suddenly brakes and everyone leans forward. Later the vehicle quickly starts again and everyone is pushed back in their seats.

- Why do you think the passengers lean forward when the bus brakes?
- What safety rules do you know that protect people in moving vehicles?

Newton's First Law is not only a classroom idea. It explains many events in daily life and guides how we design vehicles and keep people safe. In this lesson we study applications of the law and explain why it is important.

We begin with the example given in the curriculum.

pages.title: A metal ball on a smooth surface
pages.body:
A metal ball placed on a smooth surface and given a push begins to move. Because the surface is smooth, friction is small and the ball keeps moving in a straight line at nearly constant speed. It stops only when it reaches a blockade such as a wall. The wall provides an unbalanced force that brings it to rest. This shows both parts of the law.

Next we explain why seat belts save lives.

pages.title: Seat belts and road safety
pages.body:
When a vehicle moving at speed stops suddenly in a crash, the passengers inside tend to keep moving forward at the same speed because of their inertia. Without a seat belt, a passenger could hit the dashboard or be thrown through the windscreen. A seat belt applies a force that slows the body together with the vehicle. Headrests protect the neck when a vehicle is hit from behind, because the head tends to stay at rest while the body is pushed forward.

Now we study more examples from home, school and sport.

pages.title: Other everyday applications
pages.body:
- Beating a dusty cloth or mat. The cloth moves, but the dust tends to stay at rest and so is left behind.
- Shaking a bottle of sauce downwards and stopping it suddenly. The sauce keeps moving and comes out of the bottle.
- Tightening a loose hammer head by banging the handle on a hard surface. The handle stops, but the head keeps moving down and tightens on the handle.
- A runner cannot stop immediately at the finish line because of inertia and must slow down gradually.
- Loose objects such as a phone on a dashboard slide forward when the vehicle brakes sharply.
- In a vehicle taking a sharp bend, passengers feel pushed to the outside because their bodies tend to continue in a straight line.

questions.q: Explain how a seat belt protects a passenger in terms of inertia.

parts.a: In a sudden stop the passenger tends to keep moving forward because of inertia. The seat belt applies a force that slows the body with the vehicle, so the passenger does not hit the dashboard or windscreen.

ideas.t: In a sudden stop the passenger tends to keep moving forward because of inertia
The seat belt applies a force that slows the body together with the vehicle
So the passenger does not hit the dashboard or windscreen

questions.q: Explain why dust leaves a cloth when it is beaten.

parts.a: The cloth moves but the dust tends to stay at rest because of inertia, so it is left behind.

ideas.t: The cloth moves
The dust tends to stay at rest (inertia) so it is left behind

questions.q: Describe one application of Newton's First Law at school or at home.

parts.a: Beating a dusty mat, shaking sauce down a bottle and stopping, or phones sliding forward when a vehicle brakes. The object tends to keep its state of motion or rest.

ideas.t: A valid example such as beating a mat, sauce bottle, hammer head or sliding phone
The object keeps its state of rest or motion (inertia)

questions.q: A passenger in a bus moves forward when the driver brakes suddenly. This is explained by
questions.e: The driver suddenly brakes and everyone leans forward.

questions.q: Why do passengers need to wear seat belts?

parts.a: When a vehicle stops suddenly the passengers keep moving forward because of inertia; the seat belt holds them back so they are not thrown against the dashboard or through the windscreen.

ideas.t: In a sudden stop the passenger tends to keep moving forward because of inertia
The seat belt applies a force that slows the body together with the vehicle
So the passenger does not hit the dashboard or windscreen

questions.q: A driver is carrying a heavy load of sand on an open truck. Explain why the load must be covered and tied down.

parts.a: When the truck brakes or turns, the sand tends to keep moving because of inertia and could fly off. Covering and tying down the load keeps it with the truck and protects other road users.

ideas.t: Loads keep moving because of inertia when the truck stops or turns
Loose sand could fly off and harm others
Tying down and covering holds it in place

pages.body:
[[pic: Illustration of a car braking suddenly. A driver with a seat belt is held back while a dummy without a seat belt moves forward. Label inertia, direction of motion and force from the seat belt.]]

Finally we summarise why the law matters.

pages.title: Why the law is important
pages.body:
- It explains why objects behave as they do, so engineers can predict motion.
- It guides vehicle design, including seat belts, headrests and air bags.
- It explains why heavy vehicles take longer to stop, so drivers must keep a safe distance and obey speed limits.
- It explains why loads on lorries and motorbikes must be tied down.
- It helps in sports, where players use it to control balls and their own bodies.
- It is used in planning space travel, since spacecraft in space keep moving without fuel.

questions.q: State two reasons why the law is important to society.

parts.a: It guides vehicle design (seat belts, headrests, air bags); it explains why heavy vehicles need longer to stop, so drivers keep a safe distance; loads must be tied down; it is used in space travel.

ideas.t: It guides vehicle design and safety such as seat belts
It explains stopping distance, tying down loads, sport or space travel

pages.body:
Collect a magnet and a mixed set of small objects such as a nail, a coin, a pencil, a paper clip, a piece of cloth and a rubber band. Bring the magnet close to each object.

- Which objects did the magnet attract?
- What do the objects the magnet attracted have in common?

Magnets have been known for thousands of years and are now found in homes, schools, hospitals and industry. In this lesson we study what magnets are, their types, their characteristics and their uses.

We start with a simple description of a magnet and of magnetic materials.

pages.title: What a magnet is
pages.body:
A magnet is an object that attracts certain materials and produces a magnetic field around it. Materials that are attracted to a magnet are called magnetic materials. They include iron, steel, nickel and cobalt. Materials that are not attracted, such as wood, plastic, glass, copper, aluminium, paper and cloth, are called nonmagnetic materials.

Next we list the types of magnets by where they come from and by how they are shaped.

questions.q: Name four magnetic materials and four nonmagnetic materials.

parts.a: Magnetic: iron, steel, nickel, cobalt. Nonmagnetic: wood, plastic, glass, copper, aluminium, paper, cloth.

ideas.t: Iron
Steel
Nickel
Cobalt
Wood
Plastic
Glass
Copper, aluminium, paper or cloth

questions.q: Which of the following is a magnetic material?
questions.e: We start with a simple description of a magnet and of magnetic materials.

pages.title: Types of magnets
pages.body:
- Natural magnets, such as lodestone, also called magnetite, are found in the ground as a kind of rock.
- Artificial magnets are made by people from iron, steel or alloys. They may be permanent magnets, which keep their magnetism for a long time, or temporary magnets, which keep it only while in contact with another magnet or while a current flows.
- Electromagnets are coils of wire wrapped around an iron core. They become magnets only while an electric current flows and can be made very strong.

Artificial magnets are made in different shapes for different jobs. Bar magnets are long rectangular bars. Horseshoe magnets are bent into a U shape so that the two poles are close together and give a strong pull. Ring and disc magnets are used in loudspeakers and fridge doors. Needle magnets are used in compasses.

[[pic: A set of drawings of a bar magnet, a horseshoe magnet, a ring magnet and a compass needle with the north and south poles labelled and coloured differently.]]

Now we study the properties that all magnets share.

questions.q: Name two types of magnets.

parts.a: Natural magnets (lodestone) and artificial magnets, and electromagnets.

ideas.t: One type of magnet
A second type

pages.title: Characteristics of a magnet
pages.body:
- A magnet attracts magnetic materials. The pull is strongest at the ends of the magnet, which are called the poles.
- Every magnet has two poles, a north pole and a south pole. If a magnet is cut in half, each piece still has two poles.
- Like poles repel and unlike poles attract. Two north poles or two south poles push apart, while a north pole and a south pole pull together. Repulsion is the only sure test for a magnet, because an unmagnetised piece of iron is also attracted by a magnet.
- When a magnet is hung from a thread so that it can swing freely, it settles in a north south direction, with its north seeking pole pointing towards the geographic north of the Earth. This is the basis of the magnetic compass.
- A magnet can lose its magnetism if it is heated, hammered or dropped many times.
You can see the magnetic field of a bar magnet by placing a sheet of paper over it and sprinkling iron filings on the paper. The filings arrange themselves in curved lines from one pole to the other.

questions.q: State the rule about poles of magnets that attract and repel.

parts.a: Like poles repel and unlike poles attract.

ideas.t: Like poles repel
Unlike poles attract

questions.q: Explain why repulsion is a better test for a magnet than attraction.

parts.a: An unmagnetised piece of iron is also attracted by a magnet, but only a magnet can repel another magnet.

ideas.t: A piece of unmagnetised iron is also attracted
Only a magnet repels another magnet

questions.q: When the north poles of two magnets are brought together they
questions.e: Every magnet has two poles, a north pole and a south pole.

questions.q: State the law of magnetic poles.

parts.a: Like poles repel and unlike poles attract.

ideas.t: Like poles repel
Unlike poles attract

questions.q: Describe how you would test whether an iron bar is a magnet.

parts.a: Bring one end of the bar near a known magnet's pole. If it repels, it is a magnet; attraction alone is not a sure test because unmagnetised iron is also attracted.

ideas.t: Bring it near the pole of a known magnet
If it repels, it is a magnet (attraction is not a sure test)

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Magnets, Their Types, Characteristics and Uses (part 4)

pages.body:
Magnetic materials are the materials that a magnet attracts. They include iron, steel, nickel and cobalt. Wood, plastic, glass, copper and aluminium are non magnetic materials. A piece of steel can be made into a magnet by stroking it many times in one direction with one pole of a strong magnet, and it can also be magnetised by placing it inside a coil of wire that carries a direct current. A magnet can be demagnetised by heating it strongly, by hammering it, or by placing it in a coil that carries an alternating current. To keep bar magnets strong, they are stored in pairs with unlike poles side by side and a small piece of soft iron called a keeper across each end.

Finally we study how magnets are used to solve problems.

questions.q: Name three magnetic materials.

parts.a: Any three of: iron, steel, nickel and cobalt.

ideas.t: Names magnetic materials

questions.q: State two ways of demagnetising a magnet.

parts.a: Any two of: heating it strongly, hammering it, or placing it in a coil that carries an alternating current.

ideas.t: Heating strongly
Hammering
Coil with alternating current

pages.title: Uses of magnets
pages.body:
| **Use** | **How the magnet is used** |
|---|---|
| Compass | A needle magnet turns to point north and helps with direction finding |
| Fridge and cupboard doors | Magnetic strips hold the door tightly closed |
| Loudspeakers and microphones | Magnets and coils change electrical signals into sound and back again |
| Electric bells, motors and generators | Electromagnets and magnets work with coils to produce motion or electricity |
| Scrap yards and recycling | Electromagnets on cranes lift iron and steel and separate them from other waste |
| Cards and security | Magnetic strips store information on ATM and identity cards |
| Hospitals | Strong magnets in MRI scanners produce images of the inside of the body |

> **Caring for magnets** Store bar magnets in pairs with opposite poles together and a piece of iron across the ends. Keep them away from heat, do not drop them and keep strong magnets away from phones, bank cards and medical devices such as pacemakers.

questions.q: Describe two uses of magnets in everyday life.

parts.a: A compass needle points north to find direction; magnetic strips hold fridge doors closed; electromagnets lift scrap iron; loudspeakers; MRI scanners.

ideas.t: A use such as compass, fridge door, loudspeaker, crane, cards or MRI
A second use

questions.q: A learner wants to keep two bar magnets strong for a long time. Describe how the magnets should be stored.

parts.a: Store the bar magnets in a pair with unlike (opposite) poles together and a piece of iron across the ends. Keep them away from heat and do not drop them.

ideas.t: Store in pairs with opposite poles together
A piece of iron across the ends
Keep away from heat and do not drop them

pages.body:
Try to lift a heavy bag of sand straight up. Then roll it up a plank onto a table. Finally lift one end with a long stick placed over a block.

- Which method needed the least effort?
- What did each method do to make the job easier?

People have used simple devices for thousands of years to do jobs that would otherwise be too hard. In this lesson we identify the simple machines and list examples of each.

We start with what we mean by a machine and by work.

pages.title: What a machine is
pages.body:
A machine is a device that makes work easier by changing the size or direction of a force, or the speed at which work is done. In science, work is done when a force moves an object in the direction of the force. A simple machine is a basic device with few or no moving parts. A machine does not create energy. It only makes the job easier to do.

Next we list and describe each one with examples.

questions.q: Define a simple machine.

parts.a: A simple machine is a basic device with few or no moving parts that makes work easier by changing the size or direction of a force.

ideas.t: A basic device with few or no moving parts
It makes work easier by changing a force

pages.title: The six simple machines
pages.body:
| **Simple machine** | **Description** | **Examples** |
|---|---|---|
| Lever | A rigid bar that turns about a fixed point called the fulcrum | Seesaw, crowbar, scissors, wheelbarrow, broom |
| Pulley | A wheel with a rope around it that changes the direction of the force | Flagpole, well pulley, crane |
| Inclined plane | A sloping surface that lets a load be raised using less force over a longer distance | Ramp, ladder, slope, road up a hill |
| Wedge | Two inclined planes joined so that it splits or cuts things apart | Axe, knife, chisel, nail |
| Screw | An inclined plane wrapped around a cylinder | Bolt, jar lid, drill bit, screw jack |
| Wheel and axle | A large wheel fixed to a smaller axle so both turn together | Door knob, steering wheel, bicycle wheel, screwdriver |

[[pic: Six small drawings in a row of the six simple machines. A lever on a seesaw, a pulley at a well, an inclined plane as a ramp, a wedge as an axe, a screw as a bolt and a wheel and axle as a steering wheel. Label each.]]

Finally we see that many everyday tools join several simple machines.

parts.a: Lever, pulley, inclined plane, wedge, screw, wheel and axle.

ideas.t: Lever
Pulley
Inclined plane
Wedge
Screw
Wheel and axle

questions.q: Name the simple machine that is used in an axe and in a ramp.

parts.a: An axe is a wedge and a ramp is an inclined plane.

ideas.t: Axe: wedge
Ramp: inclined plane

questions.q: Which of the following is a wedge?
questions.e: Wedge   Two inclined planes joined so that it splits or cuts things apart   Axe, knife, chisel, nail

questions.q: Name the six simple machines.

parts.a: Lever, pulley, inclined plane, wedge, screw, wheel and axle.

ideas.t: Lever
Pulley
Inclined plane
Wedge
Screw
Wheel and axle

pages.title: Compound machines
pages.body:
A compound machine is made of two or more simple machines working together. A bicycle uses wheels and axles, levers in the brakes and pedals, and a screw in many of its fittings. A pair of scissors combines two levers with two wedges as blades. A wheelbarrow uses a lever and a wheel and axle.

> **Did you know?** Many farm tools used in Ghana are simple machines. A cutlass edge is a wedge, a hoe handle works as a lever, and a wheelbarrow is a lever with a wheel and axle.

questions.q: Explain why a wheelbarrow is a compound machine.

parts.a: A compound machine is made of two or more simple machines working together; a wheelbarrow uses a lever and a wheel and axle.

ideas.t: A compound machine has two or more simple machines
A wheelbarrow combines a lever and a wheel and axle

pages.body:
Two learners sit on a seesaw with a heavy one close to the middle and a light one far from the middle. The seesaw can balance.

- Why can a light person balance a heavier person on a seesaw?
- What do you think would happen if the heavy learner moved to the end?

A lever is the simplest of the simple machines and the one most used in daily life. In this lesson we name the parts of a lever, learn the three classes of levers and explain how each one makes work easier.

We start by naming the three parts that every lever has.

pages.title: Parts of a lever
pages.body:
- The fulcrum is the fixed point about which the lever turns.
- The effort is the force that we apply to the lever.
- The load is the weight or resistance that the lever moves.

The distance from the fulcrum to the effort is the effort arm. The distance from the fulcrum to the load is the load arm. For a lever that is balanced, effort multiplied by effort arm equals load multiplied by load arm.

**Effort x Effort arm = Load x Load arm**

We now study each class in turn, starting with levers in which the fulcrum is in the middle.

questions.q: Name the three parts of a lever.

parts.a: The fulcrum, the effort and the load.

ideas.t: Fulcrum
Effort
Load

pages.title: First class levers
pages.body:
In a first class lever, the fulcrum lies between the effort and the load. Examples are a seesaw, a crowbar, a pair of scissors, pliers and a claw hammer. If the effort arm is longer than the load arm, a small effort moves a large load. If the effort arm is shorter, the lever helps by changing the direction of motion or by moving the load a long way.

Next we study levers in which the load is in the middle.

pages.title: Second class levers
pages.body:
In a second class lever, the load lies between the fulcrum and the effort. The effort arm is always longer than the load arm, so a small effort can lift a large load. Examples are a wheelbarrow, a nutcracker, a bottle opener and a door opened by pushing at the handle.

Finally we study levers in which the effort is in the middle.

questions.q: Explain why a wheelbarrow makes the lifting of a load easier.

parts.a: A wheelbarrow is a second class lever with the load between the fulcrum (wheel) and the effort, so the effort arm is longer than the load arm and a small effort lifts a large load.

ideas.t: It is a second class lever with the load between the wheel (fulcrum) and the effort
The effort arm is longer than the load arm so a small effort lifts a large load

pages.title: Third class levers
pages.body:
In a third class lever, the effort lies between the fulcrum and the load. The effort arm is shorter than the load arm, so a larger effort is needed to move the load. These levers do not multiply the force but they let the load move a long distance and quickly. Examples are a broom, a fishing rod, a pair of tweezers and the human forearm when lifting a weight in the hand.

[[pic: Three simple lever diagrams side by side. First class with the fulcrum in the middle. Second class with the load in the middle. Third class with the effort in the middle. Each is drawn as a bar on a triangle with arrows for effort and load.]]

| **Class** | **Order of parts** | **Examples** | **Main advantage** |
|---|---|---|---|
| First class | Effort, fulcrum, load | Seesaw, crowbar, scissors, pliers | Can magnify force or change direction |
| Second class | Fulcrum, load, effort | Wheelbarrow, nutcracker, bottle opener | Always magnifies force |
| Third class | Fulcrum, effort, load | Broom, fishing rod, tweezers | Gives speed and a long reach |

To finish, we use the balance rule on a simple problem.

pages.title: A worked example
pages.body: A crowbar is used to lift a stone of weight 600 N. The load arm is 0.2 m and the effort arm is 1.2 m. The effort needed is found from effort multiplied by 1.2 m equals 600 N multiplied by 0.2 m. The right side is 120 N m, so the effort is 120 divided by 1.2, which is 100 N. A small effort of 100 N lifts a stone of weight 600 N.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Work Input, Work Output and Efficiency of Machines

pages.body:
Push a barrel up a ramp onto a platform. Then lift the same barrel directly. Notice how much more force you needed in the second case and how much longer the first took.

- Does the ramp reduce the amount of work you do, or only the force you use?
- If you pushed a heavy barrel up a rough, muddy ramp, would the job be easier or harder than on a smooth ramp?

Machines make work easier, but they are never perfect. In this lesson we define work, work input, work output and efficiency, learn how to calculate efficiency and see how the efficiency of a machine can be improved.

We begin with a precise meaning of work.

pages.title: Work
pages.body:
Work is done when a force moves an object in the direction of the force. Work is calculated as force multiplied by distance moved in the direction of the force. The unit of work is the joule, written J. One joule is the work done when a force of one newton moves an object by one metre.

**Work done = Force x Distance moved**

Now we distinguish what goes into a machine from what comes out.

pages.title: Work input and work output
pages.body:
- Work input is the work done on the machine by the effort.
- Work output is the useful work done by the machine on the load.

Work output is always less than work input. Some of the energy supplied is wasted in overcoming friction between moving parts and in lifting the moving parts of the machine itself, and it appears as heat and sometimes sound.

Next we measure how well a machine uses the work put into it.

questions.q: Write the formula for efficiency and state what the letters in your formula stand for.

parts.a: Efficiency = (work output ÷ work input) × 100%, where work output is the useful work done by the machine and work input is the work done on the machine.

ideas.t: Efficiency = (work output ÷ work input) × 100%
Work output is the useful work done by the machine
Work input is the work done on the machine by the effort

questions.q: The unit of force is the
questions.e: Statement of the law Newton's First Law of motion states that an object at rest remains at rest, and an object in motion continues to move in a straight line at constant speed, unless it is acted on by an unbalanced force.

pages.title: Efficiency
pages.body:
The efficiency of a machine is the ratio of its work output to its work input, expressed as a percentage. It tells us what fraction of the work supplied becomes useful work.

**Efficiency = (Work output divided by Work input) x 100%**

Because some work is always wasted, the efficiency of a real machine is always less than 100 percent. A machine with a high efficiency wastes little.

We practise with two examples.

pages.title: Worked examples
pages.body:
- A pulley system lifts a load of 120 N through 1 m. The effort is 50 N and it moves through 4 m. Work input is 50 times 4, which is 200 J. Work output is 120 times 1, which is 120 J. Efficiency is 120 divided by 200 times 100, which is 60 percent.
- A machine has an efficiency of 80 percent. If the work input is 500 J, the work output is 80 divided by 100 times 500, which is 400 J. The remaining 100 J is wasted as heat and sound.

The mechanical advantage of a machine is the load divided by the effort. In the first example it is 120 divided by 50, which is 2.4. This number tells us how many times the machine multiplies our effort.

[[pic: Diagram of a pulley system lifting a load. Arrows show effort, load, the distance moved by effort and the distance moved by load. A table beside it shows work input, work output and efficiency.]]

Finally we consider how to make machines waste less.

lessons.title: Improving the efficiency of simple machines

pages.title: Improving the efficiency of simple machines
pages.body:
- Oil or grease moving parts to reduce friction, for example the chain of a bicycle or the hinges of a door.
- Keep machines clean and free of rust and dust.
- Use smooth surfaces for ramps and slopes.
- Use lighter materials for the moving parts, when this is safe.
- Keep tools sharp, for example a cutlass or knife, so that less force is wasted.
- Service and repair machines regularly and tighten loose parts.

> **Did you know?** A perfect machine with an efficiency of 100 percent does not exist. Even the best bicycle chain loses a small amount of the energy you supply as heat through friction.

questions.q: Describe two ways of improving the efficiency of a bicycle.

parts.a: Oil or grease the chain and moving parts to reduce friction; keep it clean and free of rust; service it regularly.

ideas.t: Oil or grease the moving parts such as the chain
Keep it clean and free of rust
Service and repair regularly

pages.body:
- A force is a push or a pull measured in newtons. Balanced forces do not change motion, while unbalanced forces do.
- Inertia is the tendency of an object to resist a change in its state of rest or motion, and the mass of an object measures its inertia.
- Newton's First Law states that an object remains at rest or moves in a straight line at constant speed unless acted on by an unbalanced force.
- Seat belts, headrests, safe stopping distances and tied down loads all apply Newton's First Law.
- Magnets attract iron, steel, nickel and cobalt, have two poles, repel like poles and attract unlike poles, and point north south when free to swing.
- Magnets are used in compasses, speakers, motors, cranes, cards and medical scanners.
- The simple machines are the lever, pulley, inclined plane, wedge, screw, and wheel and axle.
- Levers have three classes, depending on the order of the fulcrum, load and effort.
- Efficiency equals work output divided by work input times 100 percent and is always less than 100 percent. Oiling and good maintenance improve efficiency.

questions.q: State one difference between balanced forces and unbalanced forces.

parts.a: Balanced forces cancel so motion does not change; unbalanced forces change the motion of an object.

ideas.t: Balanced forces are equal in size and opposite in direction, so they cancel and motion does not change
Unbalanced forces are not equal, so there is a resultant force and motion changes

questions.q: State the difference between balanced forces and unbalanced forces.

parts.a: Balanced forces are equal in size and opposite in direction so the resultant is zero and motion does not change. Unbalanced forces are unequal so there is a resultant force and the motion changes.

ideas.t: Balanced forces are equal in size and opposite in direction, so they cancel and motion does not change
Unbalanced forces are not equal, so there is a resultant force and motion changes

questions.e: When two forces on an object are equal in size and opposite in direction, they are balanced forces.

questions.q: Explain why a loaded wheelbarrow is harder to start than an empty one.

parts.a: A loaded wheelbarrow has more mass and so more inertia, so it is harder to start moving and harder to stop than an empty one.

ideas.t: It has more mass
So it has more inertia, resisting any change in motion

questions.q: Describe one activity that shows that unbalanced forces cause motion.

parts.a: Push a toy car on a smooth table: it moves when the push is greater than friction, and a harder push makes it change its motion more quickly.

It moves when the push is bigger than friction (unbalanced force); a larger force gives greater change

questions.q: State Newton's First Law of motion.

parts.a: An object at rest remains at rest, and an object in motion continues to move in a straight line at constant speed, unless it is acted on by an unbalanced force.

An object in motion continues in a straight line at constant speed

ideas.t: Inertia is the tendency of an object to resist change in rest or motion
The first law describes this behaviour

questions.q: Explain why a ball rolling on the ground eventually stops.

parts.a: Friction between the ball and the ground is an unbalanced force that acts against the motion, so it slows and stops.

ideas.t: Friction between the ball and the ground is an unbalanced force acting against the motion
So the ball slows down and stops

ideas.t: It would never stop
It would move in a straight line at constant speed

ideas.t: A moving object keeps moving at constant speed unless an unbalanced force acts
The trolley slows because of friction

questions.q: Explain how a seat belt protects a passenger in terms of inertia.

parts.a: In a sudden stop the passenger tends to keep moving forward because of inertia. The seat belt applies a force that slows the body with the vehicle, so the passenger does not hit the dashboard or windscreen.

ideas.t: In a sudden stop the passenger tends to keep moving forward because of inertia
The seat belt applies a force that slows the body together with the vehicle
So the passenger does not hit the dashboard or windscreen

ideas.t: The cloth moves
The dust tends to stay at rest (inertia) so it is left behind

parts.a: Beating a dusty mat, shaking sauce down a bottle and stopping, or phones sliding forward when a vehicle brakes. The object tends to keep its state of motion or rest.

ideas.t: A valid example such as beating a mat, sauce bottle, hammer head or sliding phone
The object keeps its state of rest or motion (inertia)

ideas.t: In a sudden stop the passenger tends to keep moving forward because of inertia
The seat belt applies a force that slows the body together with the vehicle

parts.a: When the truck brakes or turns, the sand tends to keep moving because of inertia and could fly off. Covering and tying down the load keeps it with the truck and protects other road users.
